stemMd: According to the passage, why does a squared beam often give a range of years rather than a single year of felling?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Once the beam is squared, its ring pattern tends to fit the reference sequence at more than one position.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Squared beams were usually cut from older trees, whose rings are too crowded to tell apart reliably.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Trees of the same species felled in different winters can end up showing identical ring patterns.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Squaring with an axe usually blurs the pattern of the inner rings, so the beam cannot be matched exactly.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Its outer rings have usually been cut away, so the felling year can only be estimated from what is left.

explanationMd:
Another **stated-information** question. The answer is in the second paragraph, where the passage explains why "a dated beam does not date a building".

**What to notice first.** The chain of reasoning is given in three short steps: the year of felling is known "only if the outermost ring survives"; "a squared beam has usually lost its outer rings"; so "the last surviving ring gives only a year before which the tree cannot have been felled", and researchers add an allowance for missing sapwood, "which produces a range of years".

**The step that settles it.** The correct choice compresses that chain: the outer rings are cut away, so the felling year can only be estimated from what is left, that is, from the last surviving ring; the allowance for missing sapwood is what turns that estimate into a range.

**Testing the others.** A pattern that fits at several positions would stop the dating altogether, not widen the felling year, and the passage never links squaring to a double fit. The age of the tree and damage to the inner rings are not mentioned; the axe is said to remove the outer rings. A repeated pattern from different winters contradicts the bar-code idea.

**How to check.** Read the explanation the passage gives and make sure your choice names the cause it names, not just a plausible-sounding cause.

distractorRationale.a: The passage says a calendar year can be given only when the pattern fits at one position only. A double fit would prevent dating altogether rather than produce a range for the felling year, and nothing in the passage says squaring makes a pattern fit in more than one place; in the abbey example, squared beams were dated.
distractorRationale.b: The passage says nothing about the age of the tree or the legibility of its rings, and nothing about which trees were chosen for squared beams. Squaring is described as removing wood, not as a property of old trees.
distractorRationale.d: The axe removes the outer rings; the passage does not say it blurs or damages the inner ones. In the abbey example, the last surviving rings of the squared beams were given exact years, so their patterns were matched.
distractorRationale.c: The passage never suggests that different years produce the same pattern, even within one species. It says the pattern is like a bar code, which is what allows exact placement.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying scientific passage on dating timber by its growth rings. It asks why a squared beam often gives a range of years rather than a single year of felling. The five reasons offered, in order, are: once the beam is squared, its ring pattern tends to fit the reference sequence at more than one position; squared beams were usually cut from older trees, whose rings are too crowded to tell apart reliably; trees of the same species felled in different winters can end up showing identical ring patterns; squaring with an axe usually blurs the pattern of the inner rings, so the beam cannot be matched exactly; and its outer rings have usually been cut away, so the felling year can only be estimated from what is left.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The passage says a squared beam has usually lost its outer rings, so the last surviving ring gives only an earliest year and a sapwood allowance produces a range. A, B, C and D give reasons the passage does not state. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-bocconi-verbal-logic-tila-reading-run1) reached the same answer: The passage says a squared beam has usually lost its outer rings, so the last surviving ring gives only a not-before year and the sapwood allowance produces a range. E states this. A, B, C and D (multiple fits, crowded rings, identical patterns, blurred inner rings) are not in the passage.]

review.notes: Author's uniqueness check: the second paragraph gives the cause: squaring removes the outer rings, so only the last surviving ring and an allowance for missing sapwood are available; the other choices are contradicted by the passage or unsupported by it.
